These findings were associated with considerable heterogeneity (I² = 88.27%). The prediction interval was estimated to range from 0.15 to 0.40 (Fig. 2 .A). Sensitivity analysis revealed that no individual study significantly influenced the overall effect size (Fig. 2 .B). The Galbraith plot identified Bao (2024) and Liu (2024) as potential outliers (Fig. 2 .C). Counter enhanced funnel plot suggested the presence of publication bias (Fig. 2 .D). Both Begg’s test ( P < 0.01) and Egger’s test ( P < 0.01) confirmed the presence of substantial publication bias. However, the trim-and-fill method did not identify any further studies for imputation (Fig. 2 .E). Fig. 2 Meta-analysis of the NPAR status in individuals with NAFLD compared to healthy controls. A : Forest plot analysis. B : Plot of sensitivity analysis. C : Galbraith plot analysis for identifying outlier studies. D : Counter enhanced funnel plot. E : Trim and fill plot Comparison of NAR in NAFLD and healthy individuals The metanalysis result indicated a significantly higher NAR in the NAFLD group compared to healthy controls (Hedges’s g = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.44 to 0.93, P < 0.01). Substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies (I² = 97.63%, P < 0.01) (Fig. 3 ). Due to the inclusion of only two studies, the calculation of a prediction interval was not suitable, as such intervals require a larger number of studies to provide meaningful estimates. Similarly, conducting sensitivity analyses and assessing publication bias were not feasible with this limited dataset. Fig. 3 Forest plot analysis of the NAR status in individuals with NAFLD compared to healthy controls Sensitivity and specificity of NPAR and NAR Only two studies assessed the sensitivity, specificity, and AUC of NPAR and NAR in identifying individuals with NAFLD. The results of the meta-analysis for NPAR demonstrated that the pooled AUC was 76.0% (95% CI: 66.0–86.0%) with substantial heterogeneity ( I² = 99.17%) (Fig. 4 .A). The pooled sensitivity was 69.0% (95% CI: 56.0–83.0%; I² = 99.03%) (Fig. 4 .B), and the pooled specificity was 63.0% (95% CI: 47.0–80.0%; I² = 99.38%) (Fig. 4 .C). Fig. 4 Forest plot analyses of the diagnostic performance of NPAR and NAR in identifying NAFLD. ( A ) Pooled AUC for NPAR. ( B ) Pooled sensitivity for NPAR. ( C ) Pooled specificity for NPAR. ( D ) Pooled AUC for NAR. ( E ) Pooled sensitivity for NAR. ( F ) Pooled specificity for NAR Similarly, for NAR, the pooled AUC was 69.0% (95% CI: 48.0–89.0%) with high heterogeneity ( I² = 99.93%) (Fig. 4 .D). The pooled sensitivity was 65.0% (95% CI: 49.0–82.0%; I² = 99.69%) (Fig. 4 .E), while the pooled specificity was 63.0% (95% CI: 47.0–79.0%; I² = 99.81%) (Fig. 4 .F). Discussion This meta-analysis and systematic review investigated the relationship between NPAR and NAFLD, emphasizing its potential as a non-invasive indicator for early diagnosis and disease prognosis. The results demonstrated that NPAR values were notably elevated in individuals with NAFLD compared to healthy counterparts, with a combined SMD of 0.28 (95% CI: 0.22–0.35). NPAR integrates two key physiological parameters: neutrophil percentage, reflecting systemic inflammation, and serum albumin, indicative of nutritional and hepatic status. Elevated neutrophil levels suggest immune activation in response to hepatic injury, while reduced albumin levels may indicate compromised liver function or systemic inflammation. NAFLD, a manifestation of metabolic syndrome, is closely linked to obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and endothelial dysfunction, underscoring the importance of early identification for disease management [ 40 , 41 ]. While liver biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosing hepatic steatosis and fibrosis, its invasive nature and sampling limitations make non-invasive biomarkers such as NPAR invaluable in clinical practice [ 42 – 44 ]. The NLR has also been shown to be elevated in both NAFLD and alcoholic liver cirrhosis, emphasizing the role of neutrophils in liver disease progression [ 45 , 46 ]. Inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α disrupt insulin signaling and exacerbate hepatic damage, further highlighting the inflammatory milieu of NAFLD [ 47 , 48 ]. Hypoalbuminemia, another component of NPAR, is often seen in advanced liver disease and reflects both reduced hepatic synthesis and structural alterations that impair albumin’s anti-inflammatory and antioxidative functions [ 49 – 52 ]. Furthermore, studies have identified albumin levels below 3.5 g/dL and low platelet counts as predictors of poor prognosis in NAFLD, with patients meeting these criteria exhibiting significantly reduced 10-year survival rates [ 53 ]. Elevated NPAR in NAFLD patients as a unique composite biomarker, bridges the gap between inflammation (progression of hepatic steatosis towards steatohepatitis) and nutritional status (hypoalbuminemia). by combining increased neutrophil-driven inflammatory activity Non-invasive scoring systems such as the NAFLD fibrosis score (NFS), which incorporates serum albumin, have shown effectiveness in identifying patients at higher risk of liver-related complications, while the inclusion of albumin in updated models like MELD 3.0 highlights its critical role in predicting short-term survival in end-stage liver disease [ 43 , 44 , 54 ]. Our results demonstrated that NPAR exhibited a pooled sensitivity of 69.5%, a specificity of 63.1%, and an area under the curve (AUC) of 76.05%, reflecting moderate diagnostic accuracy. Although these values fall short of the precision offered by advanced imaging techniques or liver biopsy [ 42 , 55 – 57 ], These findings underscore the potential of NPAR as a promising initial screening marker for NAFLD. Beyond NPAR, other systemic immune-inflammatory indicators, such as the NLR, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, and lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio, have also been explored for their diagnostic and prognostic significance in NAFLD [ 58 – 60 ]. Additionally, the systemic immune-inflammatory index (SII), an emerging biomarker, captures the interplay between localized immune activity and systemic inflammatory processes [ 61 ]. These markers, particularly NLR, have shown strong associations with NAFLD risk, emphasizing their potential in assessing the inflammatory environment [ 60 ]. NLR, in particular, has been suggested as a promising biomarker for predicting and preventing NASH and fibrosis in NAFLD patients [ 62 ]. Furthermore, while imaging techniques and biopsies provide comprehensive evaluations of hepatic steatosis and fibrosis, they are limited by cost and accessibility [ 63 , 64 ]. In addition to the accessibility and reducing costs in resource-limited settings, the possibility of measuring NPAR over time could provide insight into disease progression in different stages of the disease [ 63 ]. These applications underscore the potential for NPAR to enhance decision-making in NAFLD management by guiding tailored treatment strategies and frequent reassessment in high-risk individuals. This study has several strengths, notably its comprehensive evaluation of the NPAR as a potential biomarker for NAFLD. By pooling data from multiple studies, we provide a robust analysis of NPAR’s diagnostic potential, demonstrating its moderate sensitivity and specificity. These findings position NPAR as a promising, non-invasive biomarker for early NAFLD detection, especially given its ability to integrate both inflammatory and nutritional markers, which offers a unique advantage over traditional liver biomarkers. The systematic approach used in data extraction and statistical analysis, including random-effects models and sensitivity testing, ensures the reliability of our conclusions. However, several limitations must be considered. The studies analyzed in this meta-analysis demonstrated substantial heterogeneity (I² = 88.27%), which could restrict the broader applicability of the findings. Variability in patient characteristics, study designs, and methodological approaches may contribute to this heterogeneity. While the sensitivity and specificity of NPAR derived from the two studies were moderate, these values were lower than those of advanced imaging techniques and liver biopsy, suggesting the need for further refinement of NPAR thresholds. The limited number of studies included, alongside the potential for publication bias, may also impact the robustness of the conclusions. Future research should focus on validating NPAR in larger, longitudinal cohorts, establishing standardized cut-off points, and exploring its combined use with other biomarkers and imaging techniques to enhance diagnostic accuracy and prognostic capabilities. This would provide a clearer understanding of NPAR’s role in the clinical management of NAFLD. Limitations First, the included studies were exclusively cross-sectional in design, which restricts the ability to infer causality between elevated NPAR or NAR levels and the presence of NAFLD. Second, the relatively small number of eligible studies — particularly only two studies assessing NAR — restricts the statistical power, robustness, and generalizability of our findings. This limitation reflects the current state of the literature, as NPAR and NAR are relatively novel biomarkers, and more research is still emerging in this area. Third, substantial heterogeneity was observed across most analyses, including diagnostic performance metrics. We explored potential sources of heterogeneity using sensitivity analyses and Galbraith plots, and visually illustrated them in the figures. However, due to the limited number of studies, performing meta-regression analyses or formal subgroup analyses was not statistically feasible. This variability may limit the generalizability of the findings to broader populations. Fourth, demographic and geographic diversity was limited, as most studies were conducted in Asian (China, Taiwan) and Eastern European (Romania) populations. This geographic concentration may affect the applicability and generalizability of our findings to other ethnic groups and regions. Finally, publication bias was detected using Begg’s and Egger’s tests for NPAR. However, given the small number of included studies (less than ten), these tests are less reliable, and the results must be interpreted with caution. Although the trim-and-fill analysis did not impute any missing studies, publication bias cannot be entirely excluded and remains a limitation of this meta-analysis. Given these limitations, future research should focus on conducting large-scale, multicenter, prospective studies with diverse populations. Future meta-analyses should aim to perform meta-regression analyses based on factors such as age, body mass index (BMI), and disease duration. Furthermore, subgroup analyses should be conducted based on sex, NAFLD grade, and diagnostic modality to better clarify the sources of heterogeneity and improve the generalizability and precision of findings related to NPAR and NAR as biomarkers for NAFLD. Conclusion In conclusion, NPAR and NAR demonstrate significant promise as non-invasive biomarkers for NAFLD, highlighting their potential in early detection and risk stratification. These biomarkers integrate key aspects of systemic inflammation and nutritional status, which are crucial in NAFLD pathogenesis. While both biomarkers showed acceptable diagnostic accuracy, the limited number of studies, substantial heterogeneity, and evidence of publication bias warrant cautious interpretation of the findings. The clinical implications of these biomarkers are promising, yet further research is necessary to validate their utility and establish standardized thresholds for use in clinical practice. To enhance the applicability and precision of these biomarkers, future studies should focus on large-scale, multicenter, prospective studies across diverse populations. Additionally, meta-regression and subgroup analyses based on sex, NAFLD grade, diagnostic modality, and other relevant factors should be conducted to address sources of heterogeneity and further establish the clinical relevance of NPAR and NAR in the management of NAFLD. Moreover, optimal cutoff values for both biomarkers should be discovered to facilitate their accurate application in clinical settings. documents.title: Efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists in managing MALFD: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
documents.abstract: BACKGROUND: Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) affects up to 30% of the global population, yet effective pharmacological treatments remain limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonists in managing MAFLD. METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science, and Scopus, through July 2025. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) assessing GLP-1 receptor agonists or dual GLP-1/GIP GIP receptor Agonists in managing MAFLD patients were included. Primary outcomes included liver fat content, liver enzymes, and glycemic parameters. Meta-analyses were performed with subgroup analyses by receptor target, treatment duration, control type, and age. In addition, implementing a formal GRADE evaluation framework. RESULTS: Twenty-six trials involving 3,453 participants were included. GLP-1 receptor agonists significantly reduced liver fat content (MD: -3.37%, 95% CI: -4.98 to -1.76, p < 0.001), ALT levels (SMD: -0.47, 95% CI: -0.73 to -0.22, p < 0.001), and AST levels (SMD: -0.29, 95% CI: -0.53 to -0.05, p < 0.05). Significant improvements were observed in HbA1c (SMD: -0.67, 95% CI: -0.99 to -0.34, p < 0.001), fasting glucose (MD: -0.60 mmol/L, 95% CI: -0.92 to -0.27, p < 0.001), HOMA-IR (SMD: -0.34, 95% CI: -0.66 to -0.02, p < 0.05), and total cholesterol (MD: -0.23 mmol/L, 95% CI: -0.30 to -0.15, p < 0.001). Liver stiffness showed no significant improvement (MD: -0.12 kPa, 95% CI: -0.75 to 0.50, p = 0.70). Dual GLP-1/GIP agonists demonstrated superior efficacy compared to mono GLP-1 agonists for reducing liver fat (MD: -7.15, 95% CI: -10.23 to -4.07, p < 0.001 versus MD: -2.44, 95% CI: -4.18 to -0.71, p < 0.01), representing a 2.9-fold greater effect. Long-term treatment (lasting over 48 weeks) demonstrated enhanced benefits across all outcomes. Overall, changes in body weight were not significant (MD: -1.51 kg, 95% CI: -4.07 to 1.06, p = 0.25). CONCLUSIONS: This meta-analysis provides evidence for the effectiveness of GLP-1 receptor agonists in managing MAFLD, with dual GLP-1/GIP agonists demonstrating superior hepatic benefits. Long-term therapy (lasting more than 48 weeks) is necessary for optimal outcomes. These findings support clinical implementation, particularly for patients with concurrent diabetes or obesity, positioning dual agonists as promising advancements in treatment.

Abstract Background Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) affects up to 30% of the global population, yet effective pharmacological treatments remain limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonists in managing MAFLD. Methods We systematically searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science, and Scopus, through July 2025. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) assessing GLP-1 receptor agonists or dual GLP-1/GIP GIP receptor Agonists in managing MAFLD patients were included. Primary outcomes included liver fat content, liver enzymes, and glycemic parameters. Meta-analyses were performed with subgroup analyses by receptor target, treatment duration, control type, and age. In addition, implementing a formal GRADE evaluation framework. Results Twenty-six trials involving 3,453 participants were included. GLP-1 receptor agonists significantly reduced liver fat content (MD: -3.37%, 95% CI: -4.98 to -1.76, p < 0.001), ALT levels (SMD: -0.47, 95% CI: -0.73 to -0.22, p < 0.001), and AST levels (SMD: -0.29, 95% CI: -0.53 to -0.05, p < 0.05). Significant improvements were observed in HbA1c (SMD: -0.67, 95% CI: -0.99 to -0.34, p < 0.001), fasting glucose (MD: -0.60 mmol/L, 95% CI: -0.92 to -0.27, p < 0.001), HOMA-IR (SMD: -0.34, 95% CI: -0.66 to -0.02, p < 0.05), and total cholesterol (MD: -0.23 mmol/L, 95% CI: -0.30 to -0.15, p < 0.001). Liver stiffness showed no significant improvement (MD: -0.12 kPa, 95% CI: -0.75 to 0.50, p = 0.70). Dual GLP-1/GIP agonists demonstrated superior efficacy compared to mono GLP-1 agonists for reducing liver fat (MD: -7.15, 95% CI: -10.23 to -4.07, p < 0.001 versus MD: -2.44, 95% CI: -4.18 to -0.71, p < 0.01), representing a 2.9-fold greater effect. Long-term treatment (lasting over 48 weeks) demonstrated enhanced benefits across all outcomes. Overall, changes in body weight were not significant (MD: -1.51 kg, 95% CI: -4.07 to 1.06, p = 0.25). Conclusions This meta-analysis provides evidence for the effectiveness of GLP-1 receptor agonists in managing MAFLD, with dual GLP-1/GIP agonists demonstrating superior hepatic benefits. Long-term therapy (lasting more than 48 weeks) is necessary for optimal outcomes. These findings support clinical implementation, particularly for patients with concurrent diabetes or obesity, positioning dual agonists as promising advancements in treatment. Background Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) is the most common chronic liver condition globally, affecting approximately 25–38% of the global population and up to 70% of individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) [ 1 – 3 ]. MAFLD encompasses a spectrum of conditions from simple steatosis to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), which can progress to liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma [ 4 ]. This disease is closely linked with components of metabolic syndrome, including insulin resistance, obesity, dyslipidemia, and hypertension. The relationship creates a complex network of pathophysiological factors that not only increases liver-related complications but also raises cardiovascular and metabolic risks [ 5 , 6 ]. Despite the significant burden of MASH on healthcare systems, with projected increases of 63% in MASH cases by 2030 [ 7 ], therapeutic options remain limited. The current management of MAFLD primarily involves lifestyle interventions, weight loss strategies, and treatment of associated metabolic conditions. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of resmetirom in 2024 as the first specific pharmacological therapy for MASH with liver fibrosis is a significant milestone; however, access to this treatment remains restricted, and long-term clinical outcomes data are still emerging [ 8 ]. Overall, the therapeutic landscape for MAFLD/MASH continues to lack established pharmacological options for most patients, particularly those in the earlier stages of the disease or without advanced fibrosis [ 9 , 10 ]. This lack of effective pharmacological options represents a critical unmet clinical need, particularly given the progressive nature of the disease and its association with increased liver-related and cardiovascular mortality. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have emerged as promising therapeutic candidates for MAFLD due to their multifaceted metabolic effects that address several key pathophysiological mechanisms underlying hepatic steatosis and inflammation [ 11 , 12 ]. GLP-1 receptors are widely distributed throughout the body, including the liver, pancreas, gastrointestinal tract, brain, and cardiovascular system, exhibiting pleiotropic effects beyond glycemic control [ 13 ]. The hepatoprotective mechanisms of GLP-1 receptor activation include enhancing insulin sensitivity, reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis, promoting fatty acid oxidation, and suppressing of de novo lipogenesis. These effects are mediated by the modulation of key transcription factors such as sterol regulatory element-binding protein-1c (SREBP-1c) and carbohydrate-responsive element-binding protein (ChREBP). Additionally, GLP-1 receptor agonists demonstrate anti-inflammatory properties by reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines, including tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and C-reactive protein (CRP), while promoting anti-inflammatory pathways [ 14 ]. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce hepatic steatosis, improve insulin sensitivity, and attenuate liver fibrosis in various animal models of MAFLD, supporting their potential therapeutic utility in human [ 15 , 16 ]. While individual randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have suggested beneficial effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists on liver fat content and liver enzymes in patients with MAFLD, previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses have been limited by small sample sizes, limited outcome measures, and inclusion of older-generation compounds with different pharmacological profiles [ 17 , 18 ]. Furthermore, the recent development of dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonists and novel long-acting formulations has expanded the therapeutic options, necessitating updated synthesis of evidence that includes these newer agents [ 19 , 20 ]. Existing meta-analyses have not adequately addressed important clinical subgroups, such as patients with varying degrees of liver disease severity, different diabetes statuses, or different Body Mass Index (BMI) categories, which may influence treatment response and clinical decision-making [ 21 ]. Additionally, the optimal duration of treatment, dosing strategies, and comparative effectiveness of different GLP-1 receptor agonists in MAFLD populations remain unclear from existing literature [ 22 ]. The emergence of combination therapies and the recognition of MAFLD as a distinct clinical entity with refined diagnostic criteria further underscore the need for comprehensive, updated evidence synthesis to inform clinical practice and regulatory decision-making. The primary objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with MAFLD by synthesising evidence from RCTs. Specifically, we aimed to assess the effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists on hepatic outcomes including liver fat content, liver enzymes (Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT), Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST), markers of liver fibrosis, and metabolic parameters including glycaemic control (Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting glucose, Homeostatic Model Assessment for Insulin Resistance (HOMA-IR), lipid profile (total cholesterol, triglycerides), anthropometric measures (body weight, BMI, waist circumference), and inflammatory markers (CRP). Secondary objectives included evaluating treatment effects across clinically relevant subgroups defined by patient characteristics (e.g., age), disease severity, and intervention characteristics (such as drug type and duration). This evidence synthesis is critically needed to inform clinical practice guidelines, support regulatory decisions, and guide future research priorities in the rapidly evolving landscape of MAFLD. Methods Database selection and search terms A systematic literature search was conducted across multiple electronic databases including PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Web of Science, Scopus and ClinicalTrials.gov from database inception through July 2025. The search strategy employed a combination of Medical Subject Heading (MeSH) terms and free-text keywords related to three core concepts: (1) metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease [“MAFLD” OR “NAFLD” OR “non-alcoholic fatty liver disease” OR “metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease” OR “non-alcoholic steatohepatitis” OR “NASH” OR MASH OR “hepatic steatosis”], (2) GLP-1 receptor agonists [“GLP-1 receptor agonist*” OR “glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist*” OR “incretin mimetic*” OR “liraglutide” OR “semaglutide” OR “exenatide” OR “dulaglutide” OR “lixisenatide” OR “albiglutide” OR “tirzepatide” OR “survodutide” or “cotadutide”], and (3) study design [“randomized controlled trial” OR “randomize” OR “placebo-controlled” OR “clinical trial”]. Search terms were adapted for each database’s specific syntax and controlled vocabulary (Supplementary Table S1). No language or publication date restrictions were applied during the initial search phase. Reference lists of included studies, and relevant systematic reviews were manually searched to identify additional eligible studies. PICOS framework Population (P) Adult patients (≥ 18 years) with established diagnosis of MAFLD confirmed by any of the following methods: (1) liver biopsy demonstrating ≥ 5% hepatic steatosis, (2) imaging studies (ultrasound, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, or controlled attenuation parameter) showing evidence of hepatic steatosis, (3) magnetic resonance spectroscopy or proton density fat fraction demonstrating increased liver fat content, or (4) elevated liver enzymes with clinical evidence of fatty liver disease in the absence of other liver pathologies. Studies including participants with concurrent T2DM, obesity, or metabolic syndrome were eligible, provided the primary focus was MAFLDtreatment. Intervention (I) Treatment with any GLP-1 receptor agonist (liraglutide, semaglutide, exenatide, dulaglutide, lixisenatide, or albiglutide) or dual GLP-1/Glucose-dependent Insulinotropic Polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist (tirzepatide, Survodutide or Cotadutide) administered at any dose, frequency, or duration. Co-interventions were permitted if they were applied equally to both the intervention and control groups. Comparator (C) Placebo, standard care, lifestyle intervention alone, or active comparator treatments including other antidiabetic medications, hepatoprotective agents, or alternative GLP-1 receptor agonists. Outcomes (O) Outcomes included liver-specific endpoints (liver fat content measured by imaging, serum liver enzymes (e.g. ALT, AST, Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), alkaline phosphatase], markers of liver fibrosis (Fibrosis-4 Index (FIB-4), fibrosis score, and Pro-collagen type III (Pro-C3)]), metabolic parameters (HbA1c, fasting glucose, HOMA-IR), anthropometric measures (body weight, BMI, waist circumference), lipid profile (total cholesterol, High-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, triglycerides), inflammatory markers (CRP, adiponectin), cardiovascular parameters (systolic and diastolic blood pressure). Study design (S) RCTs with parallel-group design. Crossover trials were eligible if first-period data were extractable. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Studies were included if they met all PICOS criteria and reported extractable outcome data for at least one primary or secondary endpoint. Exclusion criteria were: non-randomized study designs, participants under 18 years, studies focusing primarily on other liver diseases (viral hepatitis, alcoholic liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson’s disease, hemochromatosis), studies of participants post-liver transplantation, duplicate publications or overlapping patient populations, conference abstracts without sufficient methodological detail or outcome data, post-hoc analysis studies, and studies where MAFLD outcomes were not primary or secondary endpoints. Data extraction Data extraction was performed using a standardised, pilot-tested electronic form explicitly developed for this review. All screening, data extraction, and quality assessment procedures were conducted independently by two reviewers (ST and SAA) using standardised protocols. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer consulted when consensus could not be reached. Extracted information included: study characteristics (first author, publication year, study design, geographical location), participant characteristics (sample size, age, gender distribution, BMI, diabetes status, baseline liver disease severity, inclusion/exclusion criteria), intervention details (specific GLP-1 receptor agonist, dosage, administration route and frequency, treatment duration, co-interventions and safety related outcomes), comparator details (type of control intervention, dosage if applicable), outcome data (means, standard deviations, or medians with interquartile ranges for continuous outcomes; event numbers and denominators for dichotomous outcomes), and methodological information for risk of bias assessment. Methodological quality assessment The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2 (RoB2) [ 23 ]. This tool evaluates five domains, including randomisation process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. Each domain was rated as “low risk,” “some concerns,” or “high risk” of bias, culminating in an overall risk of bias judgment for each study. Two independent reviewers conducted the assessments, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Quality of evidence assessment The quality of evidence for each outcome was systematically evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, based on the following assessment criteria: Rating down criteria Evidence quality was reduced based on five primary domains: Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB2 tool, with serious concerns (−1 point) applied when multiple domains showed “some concerns” and very serious concerns (−2 points) when studies demonstrated high risk of bias or fundamental methodological flaws. Inconsistency was evaluated using I² statistics, with moderate heterogeneity (I² 30–60%) warranting one-point reduction and substantial heterogeneity (I² >75%) meriting two-point reduction. Imprecision resulted in one-point reduction when confidence intervals included clinically unimportant effects, sample sizes fell below adequacy thresholds, or confidence intervals crossed established clinical decision thresholds. Publication bias was assessed through Egger’s regression test and funnel plot evaluation, with statistical evidence of asymmetry ( p < 0.05) resulting in one-point reduction. Indirectness was not identified as the studies directly addressed target populations receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists with MAFLD-relevant outcomes. Rating up criteria Evidence quality was enhanced when large effect sizes (standardized mean differences > 0.8 or clinically significant effect magnitudes) were demonstrated, particularly in subgroup analyses revealing substantial therapeutic benefits. Dose-response gradients provided enhancement when clear relationships existed between treatment duration and therapeutic effects. Clinical significance integration Evidence assessment incorporated established clinical decision thresholds from regulatory guidance and professional society recommendations [ 24 ]. Outcomes were classified by importance using a nine-point scale: critical outcomes (scores 7–9) essential for clinical decision-making, important outcomes (scores 4–6), and less important outcomes (scores 1–3). Quality ratings were presented using standardized GRADE symbols: ⊕⊕⊕⊕ (high), ⊕⊕⊕⊝ (moderate), ⊕⊕⊝⊝ (low), and ⊕⊝⊝⊝ (very low-quality evidence). Statistical analysis For continuous outcomes, effect sizes were calculated as mean differences (MD) when outcomes were measured on identical scales across studies or standardised mean differences (SMD) when studies used different measurement scales or units. All effect size calculations were performed using end-of-treatment values. Random-effects models were employed as the primary analysis approach, acknowledging expected clinical and methodological heterogeneity across included studies due to variations in patient populations (diabetes status, disease severity), intervention characteristics (drug type, dosage, duration), and study settings. Pooled effect estimates are presented with 95% confidence intervals (CI) and considered statistically significant when p < 0.05. Statistical heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic [ 25 ]. The χ² test for heterogeneity was also performed, with p < 0.05 indicating significant heterogeneity. Furthermore, Funnel plot asymmetry was assessed visually and statistically tested using Egger test, with p < 0.05 suggesting potential publication bias. Subgroup analysis Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore sources of heterogeneity and identify populations with differential treatment responses. Subgroup variables included: age (under 55 years, 55–65 years, over 65 year), intervention characteristics (drug type [single GLP-1 agonist vs. dual agonist], treatment duration (Short-term (24 weeks or less), Medium-term (25–48 weeks), Long-term (over 48 weeks)), and control type (placebo, lifestyle modification, active comparator). Sensitivity analysis approach Sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of findings by implementing several strategies. These included excluding studies with a high risk of bias, removing studies with extreme outlier results, using alternative effect size measures (e.g., SMD vs. MD), excluding studies that contained imputed data, limiting analysis to studies with specific participant characteristics (e.g., diabetes status), and using alternative meta-analysis methods (fixed versus. random effects). The results were considered robust if the conclusions remained unchanged across these sensitivity analyses. Protocol registration This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines [ 26 ]. The study protocol was prospectively registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; registration number CRD42024605062) before study commencement. All statistical analyses were performed using Review Manager 5.4 (The Cochrane Collaboration, Copenhagen, Denmark) and R software version 4.3.0 with the meta and metafor packages. The R scripts used for the meta-analysis and the sub-analysis are available through the GitHub repository ( https://github.com/salahalsh/GLP-1-GIP_RA_meta_analysis ). Results Study selection and characteristics Our systematic review and meta-analysis identified a total of 560 records through database searches and other sources. After removing duplicates, we screened 364 unique records for eligibility. Based on title and abstract screening, we excluded 215 records, leaving 51 full-text articles for further assessment. After reviewing these full-text articles, we found that 26 RCTs met all inclusion criteria and were included in the final analysis (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 PRISMA flow diagram showing the study selection process for the systematic review and meta-analysis of GLP-1 receptor agonists in metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease A total of 3,453 participants with MAFLD were included across 26 studies conducted in various clinical settings. These studies were published between 2013 and 2025, with half of them (13 studies) published in the last five years (2020–2025). This trend highlights the growing research interest in GLP-1 receptor agonists for improving hepatic outcomes. Most of the included trials were placebo-controlled ( n = 11, 42.3%), while the rest compared GLP-1 receptor agonists to standard care or active comparators. Sample sizes ranged from 22 to 1,197 participants across studies, with the median study duration varying considerably across the included trials. Twenty-four of the 26 studies (92.3%) had participants with type 2 diabetes, while only two studies focused exclusively on non-diabetic populations with MAFLD. Among these studies, 21 (80.8%) investigated mono-GLP-1 receptor agonists, 4 (15.4%) examined dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists, and 1 study (3.8%) compared the effects of mono versus dual approaches. The most frequently studied agents were liraglutide (13 studies, 50.0%), semaglutide (5 studies, 19.2%), exenatide (3 studies, 11.5%), and tirzepatide (1 study, 3.8%). Emerging dual agonists included survodutide, cotadutide, and efinopegdutide, each investigated in dedicated single trials. Dosing strategies varied considerably among the different agents. Liraglutide was administered at doses ranging from 0.6 mg to 3.0 mg daily, semaglutide fdoses ranged from 0.1 mg to 2.4 mg weekly, and the dual agonists were given at varying dose levels specific to each compound. The characteristics and intervention details are summarised in Table 1 . Risk of bias assessment The risk of bias assessment was conducted using the RoB2 tool for RCTs (Fig. 2 ). The overall judgements of risk of bias revealed that 13 studies (50%) were classified as having “some concerns,” while 9 studies (34.6%) exhibited a high risk of bias. Only 4 studies (15.4%) achieved a rating of low risk of bias. Fig. 2 RoB2 risk assessments In terms of domain-specific assessments, the randomisation process was generally well-conducted across most studies, with appropriate sequence generation and allocation concealment adequately reported. However, concerns were frequently identified regarding deviations from the intended interventions, particularly in studies with open-label designs where blinding of participants and personnel was compromised. Furthermore, missing outcome data emerged as a recurring issue, with several studies exhibiting substantial attrition rates or inadequate handling of incomplete data, thereby raising concerns about potential bias. The measurement of outcomes domain presented mixed results, studies that utilised objective biomarker assessments generally performed better than those relying on subjective clinical evaluations. Notably, several investigations demonstrated appropriate blinding of outcome assessors and employed validated measurement techniques. Conversely, the domain addressing the selection of reported results was relatively well-addressed, with most studies adhering to pre-specified analysis plans and demonstrating minimal evidence of selective outcome reporting. The predominance of studies classified as having “some concerns” or a high risk of bias highlights the challenges inherent in conducting high-quality research in this field. These methodological limitations were primarily attributed to difficulties in maintaining blinding for participants and personnel, particularly in intervention studies, as well as issues related to incomplete outcome data and inadequate statistical handling of missing information. Primary outcomes analysis Hepatic outcomes Seventeen studies involving 996 participants provided quantitative assessments of liver fat content. GLP-1 receptor agonists demonstrated significant reductions in hepatic steatosis compared to control interventions (MD: −3.37%, 95% CI: −4.98 to −1.76, p < 0.0001; Fig. 3 A). However, substantial heterogeneity was observed (I² = 81%), indicating variations in patient populations, intervention types, and measurement techniques. A visual inspection of the funnel plot showed reasonable symmetry (Egger’s test p = 0.26), suggesting minimal publication bias (Supplementary Figure S1A- S1K). No significant difference was observed between GLP-1 receptor agonists and control groups (MD: −0.12 kPa, 95% CI: −0.75 to 0.50, p = 0.70; Fig. 3 B). Considerable heterogeneity was present (I² = 79%), likely reflecting differences in baseline fibrosis severity and measurement techniques across studies. Twenty-one studies ( n = 1,492) reported ALT levels, showing significant improvements with GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy SMD: −0.47, 95% CI: −0.73 to −0.22, p < 0.001; Fig. 4 A). The effect size magnitude was classified as small-to-medium according to Cohen’s criteria. Considerable heterogeneity was present (I² = 82.0%), although sensitivity analyses excluding outlier studies confirmed the robustness of the findings. Similarly, AST levels from 21 studies ( n = 1,491) demonstrated significant reductions (SMD: −0.29, 95% CI: −0.53 to −0.05, p = 0.02; Fig. 4 B), representing a small effect size. Heterogeneity remained substantial (I² = 80%), with some evidence of publication bias detected (Egger’s test, p = 0.023); however, the effect remained significant in sensitivity analyses. This represents a large effect size, although considerable heterogeneity (I² = 86%) was observed among the studies, reflecting diverse patient populations and intervention protocols. The glucose-lowering effects were consistent across subgroups, although the magnitude of the effect varied based on baseline diabetes status. Insulin resistance, assessed by HOMA-IR in 7 studies ( n = 464), also demonstrated significant improvements (SMD: −0.34, 95% CI: −0.66 to −0.02, p < 0.05; Fig. 5 C), indicating a small-to-medium effect size, with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 62%). Anthropometric and cardiovascular risk factors Twenty-three studies ( n = 1,624) reported changes in body weight, showing no significant overall effect (MD: −1.51 kg, 95% CI: −4.07 to 1.06, p = 0.25; Fig. 6 A). Considerable heterogeneity was observed among the studies (I² = 92%), with 16 studies identified as outliers, suggesting substantial variation in weight responses across different populations and interventions. Waist circumference data from 11 studies with 581 participants similarly showed no significant reduction (MD: −2.22 cm, 95% CI: −4.40 to −0.05, p = 0.05; Fig. 6 B) and exhibited considerable heterogeneity (I² = 87%). In contrast, total cholesterol levels from 12 studies involving 894 participants demonstrated significant improvements (MD: −0.23 mmol/L, 95% CI: −0.30 to −0.15, p < 0.00001; Fig. 6 C). Notably, this analysis showed low heterogeneity (I² = 0.0%), indicating consistent effects across studies and populations. Fig. 6 Forest plots for anthropometric and cardiovascular risk factors. ( A ) Body weight (kg), ( B ) Waist circumference (cm), ( C ) Total cholesterol (mmol/L), ( D ) CRP levels CRP levels were assessed in five studies involving 401 participants, revealing no significant difference between groups (SMD: −0.42, 95% CI: −1.06 to 0.21, p = 0.19; Fig. 6 D). Considerable heterogeneity was also present in these studies (I² = 88%), suggesting variable inflammatory responses across different study populations. Secondary outcomes analysis Additional metabolic and hepatic outcomes were analysed across the included studies, with detailed results available in Supplementary Table S2. Notable findings included significant improvements in triglyceride levels (14 studies, MD: −0.18, 95% CI: −0.33 to −0.03, p < 0.05). On the other hand, HDL (13 studies; MD: −0.046, 95% CI: −0.11 to 0.015, p = 0.14) and BMI (18 studies; MD: −0.68, 95% CI: −1.54 to 0.18, p = 0.12) showed no significant reductions. Additionally, markers of liver fibrosis showed mixed results. The ELF score demonstrated significant improvements (4 studies, SMD: −0.57, 95% CI: −1.04 to −0.01, p < 0.05), while the FIB-4 index showed no significant change (6 studies, n = 448; SMD: −0.21, 95% CI: −0.56 to 0.14, p = 0.24). Pro-C3 levels, a marker of liver fibrogenesis, showed significant reductions (3 studies, n = 283; SMD: −0.62, 95% CI: −1.21 to −0.04, p < 0.05). Blood pressure outcomes revealed significant reductions in both systolic (6 studies, MD: −4.49 mmHg, 95% CI: −5.35 to − 3.63, p < 0.001) and diastolic pressure (5 studies, MD: −0.88 mmHg, 95% CI: −1.66 to −0.10, p < 0.05), supporting potential cardiovascular benefits of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy in MAFLD populations. Safety profile GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists demonstrated acceptable safety profiles across all 26 studies encompassing 3,453 participants (Table 2 ). While overall adverse event rates were higher compared to placebo controls, serious adverse events were infrequent and occurred at comparable frequencies between active treatments and controls. No treatment-related deaths were reported across any of the included studies. Not all studies reported quantitative rates for all safety outcomes Gastrointestinal adverse events represented the most frequent class-specific side effects, reported consistently across studies investigating both mono and dual receptor agonists (Table 2 ). Nausea emerged as the most reported adverse event, with quantifiable rates available from 17 studies (65.4% of included studies). The incidence of nausea demonstrated clear dose-dependent relationships and varied significantly by therapeutic agent. Among semaglutide studies, nausea rates ranged from 30.3% to 45% in treatment groups compared to 9.1% to 17% in placebo groups. Liraglutide studies reported nausea in 25.8% to 46% of participants, with most investigations documenting transient symptoms during dose escalation phases. Dual agonist studies revealed higher nausea incidence, particularly with survodutide (66% vs. 23% placebo) and cotadutide (ranging from 53.8% to 83.3% across dose levels vs. 12.5% placebo). Tirzepatide demonstrated dose-dependent nausea rates of 32% (5 mg), 44% (10 mg), and 41% (15 mg) compared to 12% with placebo. Additional gastrointestinal symptoms, including vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation, followed similar patterns, typically manifesting during initial dose escalation and diminishing with continued treatment. Notably, constipation was reported in 22% of semaglutide-treated participants versus 12% receiving placebo in the largest included study. Serious adverse events were systematically documented in 22 studies (84.6% of included studies), demonstrating reassuring safety profiles across therapeutic interventions (Table 2 ). The overall incidence of serious adverse events was generally comparable between treatment and control groups. Semaglutide studies reported serious adverse event rates of 7% to 13.4%, like placebo controls (8% to 13.4%). Dual agonists showed comparable patterns, with survodutide demonstrating 8% serious adverse events versus 7% placebo, while tirzepatide exhibited 15% versus 12% placebo. Additionally, the majority of liraglutide studies reported no serious drug-related adverse events, with isolated cases such as tuberculosis and migraines determined to be unrelated to study treatment following adjudication. One notable finding was the report of three malignant neoplasms in a semaglutide study (1% vs. 0% placebo); however, causality was not established given the known background malignancy risk in the study population and the limited follow-up period relative to carcinogenesis timelines. Treatment discontinuations Treatment discontinuation due to adverse events was systematically tracked across 19 studies (73.1% of included studies), with rates demonstrating considerable variation by therapeutic agent and dosage (Table 2 ). Overall discontinuation rates ranged from 0% to 18%, with most studies reporting rates below 10%. Dual agonists were associated with higher discontinuation rates compared to mono GLP-1 receptor agonists. Cotadutide showed discontinuation rates of 7.7% to 16.7% across dose levels versus 4.2% placebo, while tirzepatide demonstrated dose-dependent discontinuations ranging from 7% to 18% across dose levels compared to 2% placebo. Mono GLP-1 agonists generally exhibited lower discontinuation rates, with several studies reporting zero discontinuations attributable to adverse events. The primary reasons for treatment discontinuation were persistent gastrointestinal symptoms, particularly nausea and vomiting, occurring predominantly during the initial weeks of treatment before symptom adaptation typically occurred. Hypoglycemia and metabolic safety Hypoglycemic events were infrequent across all studies, consistent with the glucose-dependent mechanism of action characterizing GLP-1 receptor agonists (Table 2 ). Comparative studies with insulin demonstrated similar or lower hypoglycemia rates with GLP-1 receptor agonists, while placebo-controlled trials revealed minimal hypoglycemic risk in the absence of concomitant sulfonylurea administration. This finding supports the favorable metabolic safety profile of these agents in MAFLD populations, many of whom have concurrent diabetes requiring careful glycemic management. Long-term safety profile Studies with extended follow-up periods, ranging up to 240 weeks, continued to demonstrate acceptable safety profiles without emergence of new safety signals during prolonged treatment exposure (Table 2 ). Quality-of-life measures showed initial transient reductions coinciding with peak adverse event frequency, followed by recovery or improvement by study completion as adverse event rates diminished and therapeutic benefits became established. Comparative safety: mono versus dual receptor agonists Dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists were associated with higher overall adverse event rates and treatment discontinuations compared to single GLP-1 receptor agonists, primarily attributable to more frequent and persistent gastrointestinal symptoms during initial treatment periods (Table 2 ). However, serious adverse event rates remained comparable between mono and dual agonist approaches, suggesting that while tolerability may be reduced with dual agonists, the fundamental safety profile remains acceptable. Despite higher initial adverse event rates, treatment adherence remained satisfactory across studies, and most participants who continued treatment beyond the initial titration period experienced resolution or substantial improvement in gastrointestinal symptoms while maintaining therapeutic efficacy. Sensitivity analysis Sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the findings across all outcomes through a leave-one-out meta-analysis, an examination of influential studies, and outlier detection (Supplementary Figures S2A-S2K). Most primary outcomes demonstrated robust results, with findings remaining stable, even when individual studies were sequentially removed from the analysis. For liver-related outcomes, the reductions in ALT and AST levels showed robust effects, despite considerable heterogeneity. Notably, Savvidou et al. [ 36 ] and Feng et al. [ 38 ] were identified as the most influential studies for these outcomes. Additionally, reductions in liver fat content remained significant across sensitivity analyses, although eight studies were identified as statistical outliers, primarily those with larger effect sizes. However, several outcomes showed sensitivity to specific studies. For instance, liver stiffness was sensitive to the findings of Loomba et al. [ 27 ], HOMA-IR was influenced by Guo et al. [ 34 ], and fasting glucose levels were affected by Smits et al. [ 51 ]. Changes in body weight showed the highest variability, with 16 studies identified as outliers, reflecting substantial heterogeneity in weight responses across different populations and intervention protocols. An assessment of publication bias using Egger’s test revealed minimal asymmetry for most primary outcomes. Some evidence of bias was detected only for AST levels and waist circumference measurements. Subgroup analysis Target type comparison: mono GLP-1 versus dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists Dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists demonstrated substantially greater efficacy in improving liver-specific parameters compared to mono GLP-1 receptor agonists. The most notable difference was observed in the reduction of liver fat content, where dual agonists demonstrated exceptional efficacy (MD = −7.15, 95% CI: −10.23 to −4.07, p < 0.0001, I² = 51%, n = 145) compared to mono GLP-1 receptor agonists (MD = −2.44, 95% CI: −4.18 to −0.71, p < 0.006, I² = 78%, n = 714) (Fig. 7 A). This represents a 2.9-fold greater effect size for dual agonists, suggesting superior resolution of hepatic steatosis. Additionally, dual agonists significantly improved liver stiffness (MD = −4.1, 95% CI: −5.87 to −2.33, p < 0.00001, I² = 0%, n = 96), whereas mono GLP-1 receptor agonists showed an increase in liver stiffness (MD = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.11 to 0.42, p = 0.0007, I² = 0%, n = 228) (Fig. 7 B). ( A ) Total cholesterol, ( B ) Body weight Treatment duration subgroup analysis The duration of treatment has emerged as a crucial factor influencing therapeutic efficacy, with clear dose-response relationships observed across various outcomes (Supplementary Figures S3A-S3K & Table S3). Long-term treatment (greater than 48 weeks) exhibited the most robust therapeutic effects on hepatic and metabolic parameters. Body weight reduction was most pronounced in long-term studies (MD = −11.49, 95% CI: −16.77 to −6.2, p < 0.0001, I² = 47%, n = 325), representing a moderate to large clinical effect. Glycaemic control showed exceptional improvement with long-term treatment (SMD = −1.06, 95% CI: −1.41 to −0.72, p < 0.00001, I² = 0%, n = 148), suggesting sustained metabolic benefits. Notably, liver fat content reduction was significantly enhanced with long-term treatment (MD = −8.03, 95% CI: −9.83 to −6.23, p < 0.00001, I² = 0%, n = 152), representing the largest effect size observed among all subgroup analyses. This was accompanied by a significant improvement in liver stiffness (MD = −0.38, 95% CI: −0.95 to 0.20, p = 0.20, I² = 95%, n = 152) and substantial reductions in liver enzymes: ALT had an (MD = −22.88, 95% CI: −38.87 to − 6.89, p = 0.005, I² = 85%, n = 325) and AST had an (MD = −15.20, 95% CI: −29.29 to −1.10, p = 0.03, I² = 92%, n = 325). Medium-term (25–48 weeks) treatment demonstrated consistent moderate effects across multiple parameters. Total cholesterol reduction was significant (MD = −0.31, 95% CI: −0.52 to −0.10, p = 0.004, I² = 0%, n = 305), alongside improvements in AST (MD = −5.26, 95% CI: −9.97 to −0.55, p = 0.03, I² = 62%, n = 540), fasting glucose (MD = −0.71, 95% CI: −1.15 to −0.27, p = 0.002, I² = 39%, n = 206), and HOMA-IR (MD = −1.47, 95% CI: −2.80 to −0.14, p = 0.03, I² = 54%, n = 160). Short-term treatment (24 weeks or less) resulted in rapid improvements in inflammatory markers, with significant increases in adiponectin (SMD = 0.695, 95% CI: 0.434 to 0.955, p = 0.001, I² = 0%) and reductions in CRP (MD = −0.51, 95% CI: −0.62 to −0.40, p < 0.00001, I² = 0%, n = 244). Liver enzyme improvements were also evident early in the treatment (ALT: MD = −2.35, 95% CI: −4.10 to −0.60, p = 0.009, I² = 79%, n = 626). Age category subgroup analysis An age-stratified analysis revealed important variations in treatment response patterns across different age groups (Supplementary Figures S4A-S4K & Table S3). Younger patients (aged < 55 years) exhibited the most therapeutic response profile, with significant improvements across 12 different outcome measures. The metabolic effects were particularly pronounced, with substantial reductions observed in fasting glucose levels (MD = −0.36, 95% CI: −0.50 to −0.22, p < 0.00001, I² = 34%) and improvements in GGT levels (SMD = −0.705, 95% CI: −1.077 to −0.333, p = 0.0002, I² = 62.4%). Notably, younger patients showed the most significant reduction in liver fat content reduction among all age groups (MD = −3.61, 95% CI: −5.22 to − 2.00, p < 0.0001, I² = 56%) and experienced cardiovascular benefits, evidenced by a reduction in systolic blood pressure (SMD = −0.871, 95% CI: −1.673 to −0.069, p = 0.0333, I² = 90%). Middle-aged patients (55–65 years) showed a more targeted response pattern, primarily centred on hepatic improvements. The reduction in AST levels was most pronounced in this age group (SMD = −0.48, 95% CI: −0.77 to −0.19, p = 0.001, I² = 74%), along with significant improvement in the FIB-4 index (SMD = −0.976, 95% CI: −1.675 to −0.278, p = 0.006, I² = 0%), suggesting potential anti-fibrotic effects for this population. Older patients (aged > 65 years) were underrepresented in the included studies, with no significant subgroup effects identified within this age category. This highlights a potential gap in the available evidence for this clinically important population. The type of control subgroup analysis The type of control intervention significantly influenced the magnitude and pattern of observed treatment effects (Supplementary Figures S5A-S5K). Placebo-controlled studies demonstrated the most consistent evidence of therapeutic efficacy across multiple domains. Insulin resistance showed the most significant improvement (measured by HOMA-IR: MD = −2.97, 95% CI: −6.28 to 0.33, p = 0.008, I² = 63%, n = 106). At the same time, reduction in liver fat content reduction was also significant (MD = −3.97, 95% CI: −6.59 to − 1.34, p = 0.003, I² = 85%, n = 480). Improvements were also noted in liver enzymes (AST: MD = −9.69, 95% CI: −15.88 to − 3.50, p = 0.002, n = 791; ALT: MD = −10.50, 95% CI: −17.95 to − 3.05, p = 0.006, n = 792) and lipid profile (total cholesterol: MD = −0.34, 95% CI: −0.58 to −0.09, p = 0.007, n = 224). In studies using active comparators (typically other antidiabetic medications) showed distinct patterns. These studies showed particularly pronounced improvements in liver enzyme (ALT: MD = −4.54, 95% CI: −7.23 to − 1.85, p = 0.0009, I² = 94%, n = 594) and metabolic effects (fasting glucose: MD = −0.27, 95% CI: −0.35 to −0.19, p < 0.00001, I² = 0%, n = 491). These findings suggest that GLP-1 receptor agonists may offer superior hepatic benefits compared to conventional antidiabetic therapies. Comparative studies between GLP-1 receptor agonists and lifestyle interventions showed more modest but still significant improvements in fasting glucose (MD = −0.60, 95% CI: −0.94 to −0.26, p = 0.0005, I² = 0%, n = 106), indicating added pharmacological benefits. Statistical heterogeneity Heterogeneity patterns varied substantially across subgroups, providing important insights into treatment consistency. Dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist studies generally demonstrated moderate heterogeneity (I² = 55–72%), likely reflecting differences in specific agents (tirzepatide, survodutide, cotadutide) and dosing regimens. Mono GLP-1 receptor agonist studies showed higher heterogeneity (I² = 82–88%), reflecting the broader diversity of agents, populations, and study designs included. Lower heterogeneity was observed in long-term duration studies (I² = 0% for most outcomes). Age-stratified analyses showed variable heterogeneity, with younger patients demonstrating higher heterogeneity (I² = 62–92%), possibly reflecting greater diversity in treatment response in this population. GRADE quality of evidence assessment The GRADE evaluation of evidence quality across primary outcomes revealed variable confidence levels, reflecting the complex methodological landscape of GLP-1 receptor agonist research in MAFLD populations (Table 3 ). The systematic assessment encompassed critical outcome domains, with evidence quality determinations substantially influencing the strength of clinical recommendations. 17 studies encompassing 996 participants demonstrated a mean difference of −3.37% (95% CI: −4.98 to −1.76, p < 0.0001). The GRADE assessment classified this evidence as moderate quality, with initial downgrading due to substantial heterogeneity (I²=81%) reflecting diverse patient populations and measurement techniques. However, the large effect size and statistical robustness across sensitivity analyses supported retained confidence in the therapeutic benefit. Liver enzyme outcomes presented mixed evidence quality patterns. ALT reduction, supported by 21 studies involving 1,492 participants (SMD: −0.47, 95% CI: −0.73 to −0.22, p < 0.001), received a moderate quality rating despite considerable heterogeneity (I²=82%), owing to consistent directional effects and clinical relevance. Conversely, AST improvements from 21 studies with 1,491 participants (SMD: −0.29, 95% CI: −0.53 to −0.05, p < 0.05) were classified as low quality evidence, primarily due to heterogeneity concerns and marginal statistical significance. Liver stiffness assessment, derived from 6 studies encompassing 324 participants, revealed no significant improvement (MD: −0.12 kPa, 95% CI: −0.75 to 0.50, p = 0.70) and received very low-quality evidence rating, reflecting substantial heterogeneity (I²=79%) and imprecision concerns. Glycemic control parameters demonstrated the highest evidence quality within the GRADE framework (Table 2 ). HbA1c reduction, supported by 19 studies involving 1,238 participants (SMD: −0.67, 95% CI: −0.99 to −0.34, p < 0.0001), achieved high quality evidence designation despite heterogeneity concerns, reflecting the large effect size magnitude and consistent therapeutic benefits across diverse study populations. Fasting glucose improvements from 14 studies encompassing 805 participants (MD: −0.60 mmol/L, 95% CI: −0.92 to −0.27, p < 0.001) received moderate quality evidence classification, with downgrading primarily attributed to substantial between-study heterogeneity rather than effect size concerns. Body weight outcomes presented methodological challenges for GRADE assessment. Despite evidence from 23 studies involving 1,624 participants, the non-significant effect (MD: −1.51 kg, 95% CI: −4.07 to 1.06, p = 0.25) and extreme heterogeneity (I²=92%) resulted in very low-quality evidence designation. However, duration-dependent subgroup analysis revealed that this overall finding masks a significant treatment duration effect. While short and medium-term studies showed minimal weight effects, long-term treatment (> 48 weeks) demonstrated substantial and clinically meaningful weight reduction (MD: −11.49 kg, p < 0.0001), representing a large therapeutic effect. This pattern indicates that meaningful weight benefits require sustained treatment periods exceeding 48 weeks. Conversely, total cholesterol reduction demonstrated exceptional evidence quality characteristics. Results from 12 studies encompassing 894 participants (MD: −0.23 mmol/L, 95% CI: −0.30 to −0.15, p < 0.00001) achieved high quality evidence rating, reflecting minimal heterogeneity (I²=0%) and robust statistical significance, suggesting consistent lipid-modifying effects across diverse clinical contexts. Discussion This systematic review and meta-analysis, encompassing 26 RCTs, provides the most comprehensive evidence to date regarding the efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists in managing MAFLD. The findings demonstrate significant therapeutic benefits across various hepatic and metabolic parameters, particularly highlighting the superior efficacy of dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists compared to mono GLP-1 receptor agonists [ 52 , 53 ]. The primary hepatic outcomes revealed substantial improvements in liver fat content, ALT, and AST levels. However, measurement of liver stiffness did not demonstrate significant improvement, suggesting that while GLP-1 receptor agonists are effective in addressing hepatic steatosis and inflammation, their impact on established fibrosis may be limited or may require longer treatment durations [ 54 , 55 ]. Therapeutic superiority of dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists The most clinically significant finding emerged from the subgroup analysis comparing dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists with mono GLP-1 receptor agonists. Dual agonists demonstrated markedly superior efficacy across hepatic parameters, with a 2.9-fold greater effect size for reducing liver fat content and substantially larger improvements in liver enzymes. This differential efficacy pattern aligns with recent mechanistic insights suggesting that GIP receptor activation provides complementary metabolic benefits beyond those offered by GLP-1 receptor stimulation alone [ 20 , 56 ]. The synergistic effects of dual receptor activation can be attributed to distinct but complementary pathophysiological mechanisms. While GLP-1 receptor agonism primarily improves insulin sensitivity and reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis, GIP receptor activation enhances fatty acid oxidation and modulates adipose tissue function, potentially providing more hepatic protection [ 20 , 57 ]. Furthermore, preclinical studies have demonstrated that dual agonists may exert direct anti-inflammatory effects on hepatocytes through pathways that are independent of weight loss, which could explain the observed superiority in liver-specific outcomes [ 58 , 59 ]. The duration-dependent analysis revealed a clear therapeutic hierarchy, with long-term treatment (greater than 48 weeks) demonstrating the most robust effects across all outcome measures. Remarkably, long-term treatment yielded the largest effect size for reducing liver fat content, accompanied by significant improvements in liver stiffness, an outcome not observed in shorter-duration studies. This finding challenges the current clinical practice of evaluating GLP-1 receptor agonist efficacy based on short- to medium-term outcomes, suggesting that sustained hepatic benefits may require extended treatment periods [ 14 , 44 ]. The temporal pattern of therapeutic response appears to follow a biphasic model, with early metabolic improvements (such as glycaemic control and inflammatory markers) within the first 24 weeks, followed by progressive hepatic structural changes with longer treatment durations. This observation is consistent with the pathophysiological understanding that, while metabolic dysfunction can be rapidly corrected, hepatic remodelling and fibrosis regression require prolonged therapeutic intervention [ 60 , 61 ]. The current analysis substantially expands upon previous systematic reviews in several key aspects. While earlier meta-analyses by Mantovani et al. [ 21 ] and Ghosal et al. [ 18 ] included 11 and 8 trials, respectively, the present analysis incorporates 28 trials, including emerging dual agonists that have not been previously evaluated. The effect sizes observed in the current study are generally consistent with, but more precise than, previous estimates due to a larger sample size and the inclusion of more recent high-quality trials. Notably, the improvements in liver enzyme observed in this analysis (SMD for ALT: −0.47) are comparable to those reported in dedicated MAFLD? trials with other therapeutic agents but were achieved in a broader MAFLD population, including patients without biopsy-confirmed steatohepatitis [ 62 , 63 ]. This suggests that GLP-1 receptor agonists may provide hepatic benefits across the spectrum of fatty liver disease, not limited to advanced stages. Mechanistic insights and pathophysiological rationale The differential response patterns observed across outcomes provide important insights into the mechanisms underlying the efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists in MAFLD. The rapid and robust improvements in glycemic control and inflammatory markers, contrasted with the more gradual hepatic structural changes, suggest that therapeutic benefits are mediated through both direct metabolic effects and indirect consequences of improved systemic metabolism [ 64 , 65 ]. The lack of significant improvement in liver stiffness in shorter-duration studies, despite substantial reductions in liver fat content and enzymes, indicates that fibrosis resolution follows a different temporal trajectory than steatosis resolution. This finding is consistent with recent understanding that while hepatic steatosis can be rapidly reversed through metabolic improvements, fibrosis regression requires prolonged suppression of fibrogenic stimuli and activation of fibrolytic pathways [ 66 , 67 ]. The superior efficacy of dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists may be explained by enhanced metabolic regulation through complementary receptor pathways. GIP receptor activation has been shown to improve adipose tissue function, reduce adipose tissue inflammation, and enhance lipolysis—effects that may contribute to reduced hepatic lipotoxicity, independent of GLP-1-mediated mechanisms [ 68 , 69 ]. Age-related response patterns and clinical implications The age-stratified analysis revealed distinct therapeutic response profiles across different age groups, with younger patients (below 55 years) demonstrating the most benefits across 12 different outcome measures. This finding has important clinical implications, suggesting that early intervention with GLP-1 receptor agonists in younger patients with MAFLD may yield superior therapeutic outcomes compared to delayed treatment initiation [ 70 , 71 ]. The differential age-related responses may reflect several factors, including preserved hepatic regenerative capacity in younger patients, lower baseline inflammatory burden, and potentially different adipose tissue distribution patterns. These findings support current clinical recommendations for early screening and intervention in younger individuals with metabolic risk factors for MAFLD [ 6 , 72 ]. Heterogeneity considerations and clinical translation The substantial heterogeneity observed across most outcomes (I² values ranging from 63% to 94%) warrants careful interpretation of the pooled effect estimates. While this heterogeneity likely reflects the diverse patient populations, intervention protocols, and outcome measurement techniques included in the analysis, it also highlights the complexity of MAFLD as a clinical condition and the variable treatment responses observed in clinical practice [ 22 , 25 ]. In contrast, the lower heterogeneity observed in long-term studies suggests that treatment consistency improves with extended therapy duration, indicating that a longer period may be necessary for the full therapeutic effects to take place. This finding supports the need for standardised long-term treatment protocols. It suggests that clinical decision-making should take treatment duration into account as an essential factor in optimising therapeutic outcomes [ 73 ]. While the primary focus of this analysis was efficacy, the included studies consistently reported gastrointestinal adverse events as the most common side effects, with rates appearing to be dose-dependent and higher with dual agonists compared to mono-GLP-1 receptor agonists. However, discontinuation rates remained acceptable across studies, suggesting that these medications can be successfully implemented in clinical practice with appropriate patient counselling and dose titration strategies [ 74 , 75 ]. The recent approval of resmetirom for advance stage of MAFLD, with fibrosis, provides an important clinical context for interpreting these results [ 8 ]. While GLP-1 receptor agonists lack specific regulatory approval for MAFLD treatment, their established safety profile in diabetes and obesity management, combined with the hepatic benefits demonstrated in this analysis, positions them as valuable therapeutic options for patients with MAFLD who also have concurrent metabolic conditions [ 75 ]. GRADE evidence quality discussion The GRADE evidence assessment reveals a heterogeneous landscape of evidence quality across therapeutic domains, reflecting the evolving methodological maturity of GLP-1 receptor agonist research in MAFLD populations. The distribution of evidence quality ratings, ranging from very low to high confidence, demonstrates the complex interplay between statistical precision, clinical heterogeneity, and therapeutic effect magnitudes that characterizes contemporary metabolic medicine research. The achievement of high-quality evidence for glycemic control parameters, particularly HbA1c reduction and total cholesterol improvement, represents a significant methodological accomplishment in this therapeutic area. These findings establish a robust foundation for clinical decision-making, demonstrating that GLP-1 receptor agonists can reliably achieve metabolic benefits with consistent effect magnitudes across diverse patient populations. The exceptional consistency observed in total cholesterol outcomes (I²=0%) suggests underlying biological uniformity in lipid-modifying mechanisms, contrasting markedly with the substantial heterogeneity characterizing other therapeutic domains. Conversely, the very low-quality evidence classifications for liver stiffness and body weight outcomes illuminate critical methodological challenges inherent in MAFLD research. The extreme heterogeneity observed in anthropometric parameters (I²=92% for body weight) likely reflects the multifactorial nature of weight regulation and the diverse baseline characteristics of study populations, including varying degrees of insulin resistance, adipose tissue distribution, and concurrent metabolic comorbidities. This variability underscores the necessity for personalized treatment approaches and more sophisticated patient stratification strategies in future research endeavors. The predominance of moderate-quality evidence for hepatic outcomes, including liver fat content and ALT reduction, represents a pragmatic balance between methodological limitations and clinical relevance. While substantial heterogeneity prevents achievement of higher evidence grades, the consistent directional effects and clinically meaningful effect sizes support therapeutic utility. This pattern suggests that hepatic benefits, while genuine, manifest differently across patient subgroups, a phenomenon demanding more nuanced clinical interpretation rather than dismissal of therapeutic potential. Study limitations and methodological considerations Several limitations need to be acknowledged in interpreting these findings. First, the diagnostic criteria for MAFLD varied across studies, with the majority relying on imaging-based assessments rather than histological confirmation. While this approach reflects real-world clinical practice, it may have introduced heterogeneity in baseline disease severity and therapeutic response assessment [ 76 ]. Second, the relatively short follow-up periods in most included studies (median: 24 weeks) may have been insufficient to capture the full spectrum of hepatic benefits, particularly regarding improvements in fibrosis. The dramatic effects observed in long-term studies suggest that future research should prioritise extended treatment durations to evaluate therapeutic potential [ 77 ]. Third, the inclusion of diverse GLP-1 receptor agonist formulations and dosing regimens may have contributed to the observed heterogeneity. While this approach provides broad applicability, it complicates direct comparisons between specific agents and optimal dosing strategies [ 78 , 79 ]. The findings of this analysis highlight several critical areas for future research. First, dedicated long-term trials (2 years or more) evaluating dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists in biopsy-confirmed MASH populations are needed to definitively establish their role in fibrosis regression and the prevention of clinical outcomes [ 80 ]. Second, comparative effectiveness research directly comparing different GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual agonists within the same study population would provide valuable guidance for clinical decision-making. The emergence of triple agonists (GLP-1/GIP/glucagon) and novel combination therapies adds additional complexity to this therapeutic landscape [ 81 ]. Third, the development of biomarkers to predict treatment response and optimise patient selection represents a critical unmet need. The variable responses observed across patient subgroups suggest that personalised medicine approaches may enhance therapeutic outcomes while minimising unnecessary exposure in non-responders [ 82 ]. Furthermore, the results of this meta-analysis have immediate implications for clinical practice. For patients with MAFLD and concurrent type 2 diabetes or obesity, GLP-1 receptor agonists represent evidence-based therapeutic options that can simultaneously address multiple disease components. The superior efficacy of dual agonists, while promising, must be balanced against potential increased adverse events and higher costs [ 83 ]. The duration-dependent response pattern emphasises the importance of long-term treatment commitment and appropriate patient counselling regarding realistic timeframes for hepatic improvement. Clinicians should consider treatment duration as a critical factor in therapeutic planning, recognising that maximum hepatic benefits may require extended therapy [ 84 ]. Conclusion This comprehensive meta-analysis of 26 RCTs encompassing 3,453 participants provides the most robust evidence supporting GLP-1 receptor agonist efficacy in managing MAFLD. Significant and clinically meaningful improvements were demonstrated across multiple hepatic and metabolic parameters, with superior therapeutic efficacy observed for dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists compared to single GLP-1 receptor agonists. Most notably, a remarkable 2.9-fold greater efficacy for liver fat reduction was achieved with dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists compared to single agonists, positioning these therapies as potentially transformative interventions. Furthermore, duration-dependent response patterns were identified, demonstrating that long-term therapy exceeding 48 weeks is required for optimal outcomes, including significant improvements in liver stiffness and fibrosis markers. This finding emphasises the chronic nature of MAFLD, requiring sustained therapeutic intervention like other metabolic disorders. Important patient-specific response patterns were revealed, with the most comprehensive therapeutic benefits demonstrated in younger patients (below 55 years). These findings position GLP-1 receptor agonists as valuable therapeutic tools in the evolving landscape of MAFLD management, while highlighting the need for continued research to optimise treatment protocols and patient selection strategies. documents.title: Cardiovascular Disease in the Context of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD): A Comprehensive Narrative Review.
documents.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a chronic hepatic disease with a rising global prevalence (25-38% of the general population). As a new term, MASLD was introduced in 2023 to replace the previous nomenclature of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD). This new term/definition introduced changes in the diagnostic criteria and underscores the direct link between cardio-metabolic risk and this prevalent liver disease. In this context, the present review examines the clinical and pathophysiological links between MASLD and cardiovascular disease (CVD), providing a robust evidence synthesis of primarily systematic review data on the association between MASLD and coronary artery disease (CAD), atrial fibrillation (AF), and heart failure (HF). This association appears to be not only synergistic, but also independent of other known CVD risk factors, highlighting MASLD as a key cardio-metabolic risk factor that merits prompt diagnosis and treatment. The development of MASLD-related cardiovascular morbidity increases with the severity of the underlying hepatic pathology, particularly with progression to steatohepatitis and fibrosis. Notably, growing evidence highlights the links between MASLD and CVD through cardiac structural, electrical, and functional alterations that can progress to CAD, AF, and new-onset HF. Recognizing these links in clinical practice underscores the importance of early detection and multi-disciplinary management of MASLD to prevent disease progression and CVD complications.
